title: Bank-under-tile: each compute tile owns the DRAM bank beneath it
idea: Worsen: route every bit across a shared bus to a DIMM 10 cm away. Flip: hybrid-bond DRAM face-to-face onto logic at ~1 um pitch so each compute tile talks only to the bank directly below it through thousands of vertical wires, with no PHY, no shared bus and no SerDes.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): wire length drops from cm to <50 um, ~3 pJ/bit to ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit; PHY periphery area removed from both dies.

title: Charge-recycling stacked-voltage memory bus at 50 mV swing
idea: Worsen: swing every link wire rail-to-rail at 1.1 V and dump the charge to ground. Flip: stack link lanes in series voltage domains so the charge one lane releases on a transition becomes the next lane's supply, and run interposer lines at ~50-100 mV differential swing into sense-amp receivers.
why: CV^2 wall on links (facts 5, 10): 5-10x lower link energy, moving HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.4 pJ/bit.

title: Beveled-sidewall printed wiring replaces TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Worsen: drill thousands of TSVs per die so each via eats area and yield. Flip: stack thinned dies in a slight staircase with beveled edges and laser-direct-write or aerosol-jet-print the vertical bus down the sidewalls, so no die area goes to TSVs or keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers ~5-10% of die area and removes TSV-related yield loss; uses OSAT-class tools. Edge-limited wire count caps bandwidth per stack.

title: Glass-panel interposers break the silicon-interposer packaging bottleneck
idea: Worsen: make every HBM attach depend on a reticle-stitched silicon interposer from one supplier's line. Flip: build interposers on 510x515 mm glass panels with 2 um semi-additive copper lines and laser through-glass vias, giving ~8x more interposer area per panel than a 300 mm wafer and a lower-loss dielectric.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: ~3-5x lower cost per interposer mm^2, lower insertion loss trims pJ/bit; panel and PCB supply chains exist in the U.S. and allies.

title: Scatter-gather descriptor port returns only the useful bytes
idea: Worsen: open a whole 1-8 KB row to deliver one 4-byte embedding element. Flip: give the HBM base die a descriptor port where the host posts index lists; the base die activates sub-rows, gathers only the requested sectors into dense packets and ships those, so the bus carries only useful bytes.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): 4-16x fewer bits moved per useful bit for sparse embedding, graph and MoE routing workloads.

title: Progressive-precision bit-plane streaming of tensors
idea: Worsen: always send all 16 bits of every weight even when the low bits barely matter. Flip: store tensors transposed into bit planes and stream MSB planes first; the accelerator ends the transfer per tile once its error budget is met, so low-order planes move only when needed.
why: Data-movement energy and effective bandwidth: 1.5-3x fewer bits fetched for error-tolerant inference and training tensors; cold low-order planes can live in cheaper memory.

title: Passive optical multicast feeds one weight copy to many accelerators
idea: Worsen: give each of 8-72 GPUs its own private HBM copy of the same model weights. Flip: keep one copy in a pooled memory appliance and broadcast weight streams through passive 1:32 optical splitters, so every accelerator receives the same layer at once and holds only activations and KV locally.
why: Usable supply: weight replication (often 50-80% of inference HBM) shrinks by the fan-out factor, freeing HBM for KV cache.

title: Wide-slow microLED imaging-fiber links to a disaggregated memory bay
idea: Worsen: tie memory to within 5 cm of the processor so it can't be shared or cooled separately. Flip: drive hundreds of parallel microLED channels at ~2-4 Gb/s each through a coherent imaging-fiber bundle at ~0.5 pJ/bit with no DSP, so commodity DDR sits meters away in a dedicated memory bay.
why: Data movement and cost per bit: lets DDR (no 3x HBM wafer tax) feed accelerators at near-HBM energy; memory upgrades decouple from compute refreshes.

title: Command-less DRAM running a compiler-loaded access microprogram
idea: Worsen: let a controller guess access order at runtime, causing row conflicts and command-bus congestion. Flip: AI compilers know the whole dataflow, so they emit a time-triggered row/column schedule loaded into a sequencer in the memory base die; command/address pins are deleted and reused as data lanes.
why: Interface efficiency: ~20-30% more data pins, near-100% row-buffer hit rate, controller area removed from the logic die, lower energy per useful bit.

title: Self-timed delay-insensitive memory links with zero idle power
idea: Worsen: keep PLLs, DLLs and termination burning power while the link idles. Flip: use dual-rail or level-encoded self-timed signaling on short interposer links where each transfer is acknowledged by a handshake, so there is no clock tree, no training and near-zero power when no data moves.
why: Average link energy at real utilization (links idle 50-80% of the time): 2-4x lower; removes DLL/PLL periphery area.

title: Yield-elastic stacks binned by good-bank count, not die count
idea: Worsen: scrap a 12-high stack because one die has a bad bank, compounding loss with height. Flip: design the base die to remap at bank granularity across dies and sell stacks by working-bank count (e.g., 12 dies sold as 10.5-die capacity), so partially bad dies go into product instead of scrap.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6, 20-30%): recovers most stack-level scrap, roughly +15-25% sellable HBM bits from the same wafers.

title: Re-meltable laser-reflow microbumps make memory stacks repairable
idea: Worsen: bond permanently so one die failing after stacking kills the whole stack and its host GPU. Flip: join dies with encapsulated In-Sn-Bi microbumps that stay solid in operation (<105 C) but re-melt near 140 C, and use layer-selective laser reflow to lift and replace a failed die after stack test.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): converts compounding stack scrap into a rework step; reclaims good dies and the GPU, ~10-20% more good stacks.

title: Microfluidic interposer channels hold DRAM cool to cut refresh
idea: Worsen: put the hottest logic directly under DRAM so retention collapses and refresh doubles every ~10 C. Flip: etch microfluidic coolant channels in the interposer and base die between logic and memory so DRAM runs at ~45 C instead of ~90 C, stretching refresh intervals 4-8x.
why: Refresh (fact 3): refresh overhead falls from 10-20% to ~2-4% of bandwidth and idle power drops; also unblocks memory-on-logic stacking.

title: Hash-deduplicating base die stores shared KV prefixes once
idea: Worsen: store the same system-prompt KV cache separately for every user. Flip: the memory base die hashes each 4 KB block on write and keeps a content-addressed table, so identical prefix blocks across users map to one physical copy with copy-on-write, transparent to the host.
why: Usable capacity: 2-5x more effective KV capacity per GB for chat inference with shared prompts and agents.

title: Socketed HBM-class modules that outlive three GPU generations
idea: Worsen: solder memory to the GPU so it is scrapped whenever compute retires after 3-4 years. Flip: mount HBM stacks on a compression-mount, fine-pitch land-grid module beside the processor on a glass substrate, so memory is reused across accelerator generations and later redeployed into CXL expanders.
why: Usable supply: 2-3x memory service life means far fewer new bits needed per year and creates a secondary HBM market.

title: Multi-carrier RF signaling stacks channels on each interposer wire
idea: Worsen: let each interposer wire carry one baseband NRZ stream, so bandwidth is bump-limited. Flip: modulate 3-4 mm-wave carriers (20-80 GHz) plus baseband onto each low-loss transmission line with on-die filters, multiplying bandwidth per wire without adding bumps or TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax and periphery (facts 6, 7): 3-4x bandwidth per bump, so fewer TSVs or narrower stacks deliver the same bandwidth.

title: Through-silicon optical vias link stacked dies with infrared light
idea: Worsen: punch copper TSVs through every die. Flip: silicon is transparent above ~1.1 um, so bond micro-VCSEL and photodetector pairs on each die and send data vertically through the bulk silicon at 1.3 um through thinned windows, with no holes drilled at all.
why: TSV tax and yield (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area or via yield loss; short vertical optical hops at ~0.3 pJ/bit.

title: One end-to-end ECC codeword from cell to core
idea: Worsen: re-encode data at every hop, with on-die ECC, link CRC, controller ECC and cache ECC each adding bits and latency. Flip: generate one strong codeword when data enters the array, ship its raw parity bits over the link and decode only once in the processor, deleting link and on-die ECC logic.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and bandwidth: ~6-12% bandwidth and several % of die area recovered; one stronger code tolerates weaker cells and relaxes refresh.

title: Reduce-on-the-wire: interposer repeaters sum partial results in flight
idea: Worsen: write every partial sum to memory and read it back at each all-reduce step. Flip: put small adder-repeaters at segment boundaries of long active-bridge wires so gradients and partial dot products accumulate as they travel between chiplets, and only the final sum is written to memory.
why: Data movement: all-reduce memory traffic cut by ~N contributors, shrinking HBM bandwidth and gradient-buffer capacity needs.

title: Quantize-on-write base die stores KV at 4 bits transparently
idea: Worsen: store every KV value at FP16 although attention tolerates far less. Flip: the HBM base die applies per-block scaled 4-bit quantization with outlier side tables on write and dequantizes on read, so the host still sees FP16 while the array holds ~3.5x more tokens.
why: Usable capacity and bandwidth: ~3-4x more KV per GB and ~3x fewer array bits moved per token.

title: Wafer-on-wafer DRAM-on-logic accelerators with no package wiring
idea: Worsen: dice wafers, then reconnect chips with long package wires on CTE-mismatched substrates. Flip: hybrid-bond a whole DRAM wafer onto a whole logic wafer (all silicon, CTE-matched) with redundant tiles, so every logic tile has its own memory slab above it and package-level interconnect disappears.
why: Data movement (~0.05 pJ/bit vertical) and packaging cost: no interposer, no HBM base dies, no TSV stacks; yield handled by tile redundancy.

title: 77 K liquid-nitrogen memory packages with minute-long retention
idea: Worsen: run DRAM hot so leakage forces 32-64 ms refresh. Flip: immerse memory packages and interposers in liquid nitrogen, where junction leakage falls by orders of magnitude (retention of minutes) and copper resistance drops ~6x, so refresh nearly vanishes and long links get cheaper.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and data movement: refresh power near zero, lower wire energy; LN2 is made from air anywhere, unlike scarce helium.

title: Onshore HBM stacking hubs using imported known-good DRAM wafers
idea: Worsen: keep all HBM stacking and advanced packaging in one region so one disruption halts AI memory. Flip: fund U.S. packaging hubs that import known-good DRAM wafers and do TSV reveal, hybrid bonding, stacking and test domestically, since a packaging line costs ~$1-3B versus $15B+ for a fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply security within ~2 years instead of 5; captures ~20-30% of HBM value-add and seeds a later fab.

title: Fiber-loop weight carousel stores model weights as light in flight
idea: Worsen: park every weight in a leaky capacitor and drag it across a bus each token. Flip: inference reads all weights in the same order every token, so keep them circulating in a 64-wavelength fiber loop with in-line amplification and periodic electronic regeneration (a 100 km loop holds ~0.8 GB); accelerators tap each layer as it passes.
why: No capacitor or refresh for streaming weights; capacity scales with cheap fiber length instead of wafers, and latency equals loop period (~0.5 ms), acceptable for per-token weight streaming.

title: Active mature-node interposer packed with SRAM becomes the L4
idea: Worsen: waste a 2,500 mm^2 silicon interposer as passive copper. Flip: make the interposer an active 28-16 nm die from U.S. mature fabs, filled with SRAM banks under the routing, so the passive area becomes ~1-2 GB of latch-based buffer between HBM and logic.
why: Data movement and DRAM demand: hot working sets served at ~0.2 pJ/bit, cutting HBM traffic 30-50% with no capacitor and no EUV.

title: Display fabs build IGZO gain-cell memory into glass interposers
idea: Worsen: allow only memory fabs with 75:1 capacitor etch to make working memory. Flip: Gen-8.5 display fabs already pattern billions of IGZO TFTs on 2.2x2.5 m glass, so build 3T gain cells (charge held on a read transistor's gate, no capacitor) in the glass interposer's layers, turning the substrate under the chips into seconds-retention memory.
why: Capital and scarce-resource intensity: uses surplus display-fab capacity instead of DRAM fabs; IGZO leakage <1e-19 A/um nearly kills refresh. Density is low (tens to hundreds of MB per interposer).

title: Maskless e-beam via-ROM dies hold frozen model weights
idea: Worsen: keep read-only inference weights in refresh-hungry DRAM. Flip: make generic ROM wafers on a mature node where one via layer encodes the bits (multi-size vias for 2 bits/cell), and write that layer per model with multi-beam e-beam direct-write, so a weight die needs no capacitor, no refresh and no custom mask.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and DRAM demand: weights are often 50-80% of inference memory; 28 nm ROM at ~4F^2 is ~3-5x cheaper per bit than DRAM and needs no EUV.

title: Store tokens, not KV: base-die engines recompute keys and values
idea: Worsen: hold gigabytes of KV cache per long conversation in capacitors. Flip: keep only token IDs (2 bytes per token) plus sparse activation checkpoints, and let matrix engines in the memory base die regenerate K and V for evicted spans on demand, trading cheap FLOPs for scarce bits.
why: Capacity: KV per token (~100 KB+ in large models) collapses to bytes plus checkpoints, 10-100x less memory for long contexts at some recompute energy.

title: High-bandwidth flash stacks feed read-mostly weights through SRAM staging
idea: Worsen: keep weights written once a month in memory built for endless writes. Flip: stack charge-trap NAND dies with many small planes in the HBM footprint, read them wide and in parallel into a base-die SRAM staging buffer, and serve weights from there, leaving DRAM only for KV and activations.
why: Cost per bit: NAND is ~10-20x cheaper per bit than HBM; endurance is irrelevant for weights and deterministic streaming hides flash latency.

title: MgB2 flux-loop memory banks linked to processors by fiber
idea: Worsen: store bits as charge that leaks at room temperature. Flip: store bits as a persistent single-flux-quantum current in MgB2 superconducting loops at ~20 K, cooled by closed-cycle cryocoolers rather than liquid helium, and link them to room-temperature processors over fiber with cryogenic photodetectors driving the inputs.
why: Zero leakage, attojoule switching and no refresh; avoids the helium chokepoint by using a 39 K superconductor. Cryocooler wall-plug cost is the risk.

title: Domain-wall racetrack shift registers in interposer back-end layers
idea: Worsen: give random-access cells to data that is always read in sequence. Flip: deposit magnetic nanowire racetracks in the interposer back-end, where current pulses shift domain walls past one read/write head per track, so weights and activations stream out with no capacitor and no transistor per bit.
why: Density and cost: one access device per hundreds of bits on a BEOL-only process, no refresh; suited to streaming tensors.

title: Selector-only memory fills TSV keep-out and PHY back-end areas
idea: Worsen: leave TSV keep-out zones and the space above PHYs as dead silicon. Flip: build stacked layers of chalcogenide selector-only memory (threshold set by write polarity, one two-terminal device per bit) in the BEOL above these regions, adding cross-point bits on area that today stores nothing.
why: Density from wasted area (facts 6, 7): ~20-30% of base and core die area gains 2-4 memory layers with no capacitor and no front-end steps.

title: Tunnel-diode Goto pairs as two-device latches in the base die
idea: Worsen: need a giant capacitor because a bit cannot hold itself. Flip: use a Goto pair (two series tunnel diodes whose N-shaped I-V curve gives two stable midpoint voltages) plus one access transistor, so each bit self-latches like SRAM with 3 devices instead of 6, built vertically in the base die.
why: Refresh-free and ~2-3x denser than SRAM; tunnel-diode peak-to-valley ratio sets standby power, which is the main risk.

title: Layer-sharded wafer-scale SRAM: weights stay put, activations flow
idea: Worsen: give every chip a full model copy in external DRAM. Flip: assign each transformer layer's weights to the SRAM of one chiplet on a wafer-scale glass panel and pass activations chip-to-chip over millimeter wires, so weights never move and no external DRAM holds them.
why: Data movement: weights are stationary and only activations move (~100x less traffic); removes DRAM for weights using mature SRAM processes.

title: Optically bistable microrings buffer packets inside photonic interposers
idea: Worsen: convert every optical packet to electrons and park it in DRAM for microseconds. Flip: use carrier- or thermo-optically bistable silicon microrings, where a holding beam keeps each ring in one of two transmission states, as nanosecond photonic latches that buffer packets in the optical domain.
why: Data movement: avoids the O-E-O plus DRAM round trip (~10-20 pJ/bit) for switch and link buffers; no capacitor, small capacity.

title: VO2 Mott hysteresis gives a one-element volatile latch
idea: Worsen: require a capacitor to remember a bit. Flip: bias a nanoscale VO2 element inside its insulator-metal hysteresis window, where it stays either metallic or insulating; a short pulse flips it and a small read current senses resistance, giving a one-resistor-one-selector latch stacked in the link die BEOL.
why: Near cross-point density, refresh-free while biased, nanosecond switching and high reported endurance; holding current is the energy risk.

title: Diffractive glass plates bake frozen model weights into optics
idea: Worsen: store weights as bits and haul them to compute billions of times. Flip: for frozen layers such as embeddings and early encoders, etch the weight matrix as phase patterns into stacked glass diffractive plates so the matrix-vector product happens as light passes through; the weights are geometry, needing no memory or data movement.
why: Removes weight storage and movement for fixed layers; glass lithography is cheap and available in the U.S. Precision and reconfigurability are the risks.

title: Injection-locked ring-oscillator phase stores bits inside link retimers
idea: Worsen: use leaky charge to store a bit. Flip: store each bit as the 0-or-pi phase of a sub-harmonically injection-locked CMOS ring oscillator, reviving Goto's parametron inside link retimers where clocks already run, and read it by phase comparison.
why: Capacitor-free elastic buffers built from inverters only; refresh-free while clocked. Small capacity and active power limit it to link buffering.

title: Open UCIe memory-chiplet standard lets any logic fab make memory
idea: Worsen: let memory supply depend on three firms because only they can build the capacitor. Flip: publish an open memory-chiplet standard (UCIe-based protocol, bump map, test and thermal envelope) for capacitorless dies such as SRAM, gain-cell, ROM and flash, so mid-size logic fabs can sell interchangeable memory chiplets.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply: brings dozens of logic fabs into memory supply and makes them compete on cost per bit.

title: Take-or-pay offtake converts idle U.S. mature fabs to memory chiplets
idea: Worsen: let U.S. 65-28 nm fabs sit underused while memory is short. Flip: government and hyperscaler consortia sign 7-year take-or-pay contracts for capacitorless memory chiplets from those fabs, funding hybrid-bond and stacking add-ons (~$0.3-1B per site) instead of $15B DRAM fabs.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. share: adds bit capacity on depreciated tools with no EUV and no tungsten-heavy capacitor stack.

title: Sixteen-high hybrid-bonded SRAM cube in the HBM footprint
idea: Worsen: accept that SRAM is too sparse to matter. Flip: thin 16 mature-node SRAM dies to ~20 um and hybrid-bond them face-to-back at ~1 um pitch with dense through-vias, so a cube in the HBM footprint holds ~1-2 GB of nanosecond, refresh-free memory.
why: Capacity tier without capacitors: ~2 GB at ~0.1 pJ/bit and 5-10x lower latency than HBM, buildable in mature U.S. fabs.

title: Nondestructive-read multicast: one row read serves many requesters
idea: Worsen: use destructive reads so every read is written back and each requester triggers its own activation. Flip: with capacitorless nondestructive cells (gain cells, SRAM), let the interface broadcast one row read to all subscribed chiplets via a multicast tag, with no restore phase.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): restore energy removed and shared data read once instead of N times, up to Nx bandwidth gain for shared weights.

title: Pool every switch FIFO and retimer buffer into network memory
idea: Worsen: let every switch, retimer and NIC hold its own idle SRAM FIFOs. Flip: expose the tens of MB of SRAM buffering in a rack's switches and CXL retimers as an addressable, latency-tagged pool for in-flight tensors, so data in transit lands in the network instead of DRAM.
why: Usable memory: reclaims stranded SRAM (GBs per rack) for collective and staging buffers and avoids DRAM round trips.

title: Microfabricated ferrite-core planes plated onto package substrates
idea: Worsen: make memory require the most advanced lithography. Flip: plate few-micron NiZn-ferrite or permalloy micro-toroids on organic or glass substrate panels, threaded by lithographic X/Y/sense lines, reviving core memory with PCB-class tools: no capacitor, no transistor per bit, unlimited endurance.
why: Scarce-resource and U.S. manufacturability: panel processes, no EUV; low density (~50 MB per layer per 100 cm^2) suits persistent buffers and tables.

title: Refresh-free cells let memory sit directly on hot logic
idea: Worsen: never stack memory on logic because heat wrecks DRAM retention. Flip: since SRAM and ROM hold state at 105 C+ without refresh, bond them directly on the hottest compute tiles with a copper thermal-pillar grid through the memory, and push any DRAM to the cooler package edge.
why: Data movement: the nearest memory tier sits at ~0 mm, and the thermal budget no longer couples to retention or refresh.

title: Inline compute in CXL switches streams flash data, never landing
idea: Worsen: copy every dataset from SSD into DRAM, then to the GPU, then back. Flip: put streaming engines (decompress, filter, tokenize, embedding lookup) inside the PCIe/CXL switch so data flows flash to switch to accelerator SRAM at line rate and never lands in DRAM bounce buffers.
why: Data movement and DRAM demand: removes bounce buffers (tens of GB per server) and 2-3 copies per byte.
